vt.analysis:
Type: OpenClaw Skill
Name: lobstercash
Version: 0.0.3

The lobstercash skill bundle provides a legitimate interface for the Lobster Cash CLI (@crossmint/lobster-cli) to manage crypto payments and virtual credit cards. The instructions consistently emphasize a human-in-the-loop (HITL) security model, requiring the agent to provide approval URLs to the user for sensitive actions such as wallet setup, fund deposits, and card creation. No evidence of data exfiltration, obfuscation, or malicious prompt injection was found; the code and documentation are strictly aligned with the stated purpose of enabling secure agent-led financial transactions.

llm.summary: The skill's purpose (making payments, issuing virtual cards, sending crypto) aligns with its instructions, but it tells the agent to fetch and run a third‑party CLI (via npx/npm) and to reveal highly sensitive payment credentials — behaviors that warrant caution before installing.

dimensions.detail: The name/description match the instructions: the skill is a payment/wallet helper that uses a CLI to browse store items, create virtual cards, request deposits, send tokens, sign transactions, and perform x402 payments. No unrelated credentials or binaries are requested in the metadata, which is consistent with the design of using an external CLI and human approval flows.
dimensions.label: Purpose & Capability
dimensions.name: purpose_capability

dimensions.detail: The SKILL.md instructs the agent to run external CLI commands (e.g. 'npx @crossmint/lobster-cli' or 'lobstercash <command>') and to display/handle approval URLs and to reveal virtual card credentials (card number, CVC, expiry). While the instructions emphasize human-in-the-loop approval, they explicitly direct retrieval and handling of extremely sensitive payment data and to execute operations that move real funds. These actions are high-risk if the fetched CLI or the agent is compromised or if the agent exfiltrates revealed credentials.
dimensions.label: Instruction Scope
dimensions.name: instruction_scope

dimensions.detail: There is no formal install spec in the registry, but the runtime instructions tell the agent/user to run 'npx @crossmint/lobster-cli' or 'npm install -g @crossmint/lobster-cli'. That causes network downloads and execution of third-party code at runtime. Because the registry metadata and homepage are unknown and no local code is provided for review, this dynamic install increases risk — you cannot statically audit what will run.
dimensions.label: Install Mechanism
dimensions.name: install_mechanism

dimensions.detail: The skill declares no environment variables or credentials, which superficially reduces risk. However, it operates on highly sensitive resources (payment instruments, wallet balances, card credentials) and depends on an external CLI that likely requires authentication/consent URLs. The skill doesn't explain how 'agent-id' is provisioned or validated, and there is no declared primary credential despite interacting with real payment flows. That lack of explicit credential handling is worth clarifying before use.
dimensions.label: Credentials
dimensions.name: environment_proportionality

dimensions.detail: The skill is not always-enabled and is user-invocable. It does not request persistent privileges in the metadata. The instructions avoid autonomous polling for approvals and insist on human confirmation, which reduces the chance of silent writes. Still, because the agent can be invoked autonomously platform-wide, combining that capability with money-moving commands could increase blast radius — but autonomous invocation alone is not flagged per the evaluation rules.
dimensions.label: Persistence & Privilege
dimensions.name: persistence_privilege

llm.guidance: This skill legitimately provides payment and wallet functions, but it requires running a third‑party CLI (via npx/npm) which will download and execute code you cannot review from the skill package. Before installing or using it: 1) verify the CLI package (@crossmint/lobster-cli) on npm/github and review its maintainers and code; 2) prefer running the CLI yourself (manual install) rather than letting an agent run npx automatically; 3) confirm how agent-id is managed and restrict agent autonomy for money actions (require explicit human approval every time); 4) never paste private keys or other secrets into the agent; treat any revealed virtual card credentials as highly sensitive and only use them in a trusted checkout flow; 5) if you can't verify the upstream CLI or its publisher, decline installation — the money-moving capability plus dynamic code download is the main risk. Additional info (package homepage, repository, or the actual CLI binary) would raise confidence and could change this assessment to benign.
